title: Do you do anything interesting with inventory? If so, how?

posts.author: RaoHolythorne
posts.body:
I think inventory is a huge issue in RPGs, and JRPGs have traditionally just kind of ignored the mechanic in favor of a "Bag of Holding, don't worry about it" style of play.
In the early days, inventory seems to have been a huge mechanic in RPGs that most players found tedious and so just ignored: I'm talking about old school Dungeons and Dragons where a lot of the gameplay can feel like it's based on real life military experience, and this makes sense being that you had veterans like Tim Kask and Gary Gygax creating the system. I'm not sure who else served or to what extent, but I know Gary was a Marine for a little while until he was kicked out because of a knee injury, and I remember Tim Kask talking about being involved with Vietnam, though I don't recall to what extent. Then you have stories like
Fantasy F*ing Vietnam
where this idea really comes to life.
I think the majority of players didn't like the tedious nature of using "Tenser's Floating Disk" to haul all of their loot out of the halls of the frost giant jarl or making lists and keeping track of everything that they have. Especially on paper, all of this book keeping can be tedious especially when you just want to roll dice.
Enter the JRPG.
I think a lot of the early inventory limits in JRPGs had more to do with hardware than anything. This isn't an in depth, historical retrospective, so I'm going to focus on two of the ideas that I think were really cool, and I can't believe there's not an easy way to implement them into RPG Maker. Or, maybe I'm just dumb.
Final Fantasy I might be the most dungeon crawling out of all the FF games. There's a huge emphasis on resources, equipment, and carrying capacity that you really stop seeing after the first game. Really, outside of FFI, I almost never use healing items in Final Fantasy except for the occasional phoenix down. FFVIII might be an exception since, let's face it, the number of people who actually use magic in that game is pretty small.
I love how in FFI each character has four slots to load out with, and you can kind of put anything into these slots, but your equipment takes up room too. Later in the game, you get powerful magic items that you can use in battle. In order to make use of them, you need to keep them on the character, but they don't have to be equipped. This means a character like the Fighter/Knight probably won't be carrying these items because he really needs his equipment slots (weapon, armor, helmet, shield: that's all four). But, then you have a character like the Black Belt/Master who uses almost no equipment (if I recall correctly, he'll usually just use one slot for some kind of armor). That means a little extra room for carrying stuff places.
How could you implement a similar system into RPG Maker?
DragonQuest VIII does something similar. At this point in JRPGs, the dungeon crawling is starting to become vestigial: once you get to a point where resources have no scarcity, you've really left dungeon crawling country in my opinion. That said, they still had a neat inventory system that factored into combat really well. DQVIII has the traditional equipment system: put the gear on the characters and go for it. But, each character kind of has their own pack you can load out with extra tools: usually, this will end up being some secondary weapons if you're not focusing on just one (usually people focus on just one though, I think) or some emergency herbs for healing and such. Yes, you can switch equipment in the middle of a fight. I think later games in the series have the same mechanics, but I honestly don't remember even though I've beaten IX and XI.
Later in DQVIII, you'll get the same kind of magic items that you can use in battle to cast spells or create unique effects. Same idea as FFI, but with more versatility.
Hear me out now: Darkest Dungeon is an RPG where you play as the human resources manager for an estate, and you have to send your human resources into the dark dungeons to bring back material resources so you can continue to live your best life in HR.
Okay, so it's not really an RPG by most people's standards, but the reason I bring it up is because as I mentioned earlier, RPGs started out as dungeon crawlers almost first and foremost. As they became more heroic, you started getting a lot of items/mechanics that handwaved the mundane problems you would face actually patrolling through a dungeon ... or the jungles of Vietnam.
Imagine the Virgin "I can only carry so much" vs the Giga Chad "Weight? What's that lol?"
I like Darkest Dungeon. If you haven't played it, you have one big inventory, and by big I mean it's got like 16 slots. Before you go into a dungeon, you're going to go to the Provisioner and pick up rations, torches, and whatever else you think you might need. If you bring too much, you're not going to be able to bring back as much loot. If you don't bring enough, you might not bring back any loot at all.
I like dungeon crawling. I like games like Chained Echoes where resource management isn't really a mechanic. I think both are great.
For my project, I'm trying to find a way to lean more into a dungeon crawling inventory system. I think it's a big mistake or at least missed opportunity for emersion and challenge to just give players room to carry 99 potions so they can heal up whenever. I like how Chained Echoes realized this was a boring way to do things and just healed characters up after every encounter, but I don't want to do that. I want a dash more Fantasy Vietnam. Not too much. Just a little. Why? Well, I'm actually a soldier, and I think the idea of having virtually unlimited resources on a patrol loses a lot of the meaning in the struggle.
One of my favorite feelings in a JRPG is when you go from "I don't know if we're going to make it" to "Oh man, we made it! What a relief!"
CONCLUSION:
So, what kind of interesting things do you do with inventory in RPG Maker? I've been trying some ideas out; I implemented
Galv's Actor Equip Items
, and it doesn't do everything I want, but I at least like the utility of limiting items for combat, and I'm trying to think of more limitations I can implement to increase the challenge of my dungeons. In old school TTRPGs, the dungeon itself
is
the boss. Each encounter is a tax you pay or avoid on your way to scoring a big haul. I like that, but I'm struggling to implement the idea with RPG Maker.
First time posting on the forums. I post on Reddit every now and then, but the community over there is pretty lackluster in my opinion. I hope I'm posting the right way in the right place, and I really hope I spark an interesting discussion everyone can get some ideas from. Thank you for reading!

posts.author: LordOfPotatos
posts.body:
the problem with more complex inventory systems is the menuing. they rarely add any strategic depth that's actually worth all the time you'll spend managing character inventories.
the best approach IMO is individual item limits like tales of does. you can carry infinite items, but only a certain number of each item.
10 potions, 5 megapotions, 1 elixir, 99 mushrooms etc.
this approach kills all the birds with 1 stone: you get the tension of running out of supplies because you can only stack so many, the convenience of infinite inventory slots for crafting materials and other things, and you can use the inventory limit to balance things like elixirs and eliminate JRPG hoarding, and the inventory management is kept at a minimum.

posts.author: Nerooo
posts.body:
Item/Gold management is a big part of my project. I even feature a class (Craftsman) that can convert gold into MP, combine items into new ones, use gold to power up items, whack people with the bag with more power the more items and gold you're carrying, etc.
I use a single inventory for the party with 50 slots, no item stacking. I'm working on making it a grid instead of a list to make navigation easier and faster.
Key Items are kept in a separate inventory.
I also reduced the amount of loot drops from enemies, with each enemy featuring a regular drop (you always get it from defeating one) and a rare drop (you need to defeat them with a specific element/status effect/condition for it to drop).
I also made items less common in dungeons. Instead of collecting random trash, you only collect stuff with value, like rare weapons, a particularly rare material or a strong consumable item. Treasure chests are rare and usually hidden, they may contain up to 5 items and some gold.
The player's HUB area, the Airship, has a vault that can store up to 999 items, so you want to gather valuables in your exploration and store them in the vault for later.
Overall I think that the secret to making items interesting is balancing rarity/usefulness. If items are common you need to make them weaker. If items are rarer you need to make them more powerful to compensate. I try to make finding a new item/chest a highlight of that exploration, instead of something you do a dozen times back to back.
Quality over Quantity.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
in my project, the player's party comp is a thing that i give free reign over once they unlock the classes. a party of 4 where each character has a main class and a sub class with a total of 40 classes ingame presents "a few" comps. For the most part, i don't design encounters with the assumption that the player is using any class. One of my goals for the game is to not make the game feel overly punishing towards certain classes on a general level. Inventory at some point became a part of it as it changed from being a resource that fills the gap to literally being how some classes function.
I cap the number of healing items on an item by item basis. For example, you only get to hold 2 Megalixirs, 8 High-Potions, and 15 Throwing Knives, etc.. No consumable is particularly rare and all can be bought somewhere, but you cant hold too many of each at a time. but since some classes want to go out of their way to use more items than others it ends up feeling tighter with them around.
My current solution was having the classes directly impact the item economy. a few examples
-Thieves are able to turn buff items AOE by using 4 at a time to buff all 4 party members, so they have a chance to not consume buff items in general when they use them.
-Having Medics in the party increases the cap of each healing item by a specific amount per medic because they naturally heal more with items and they consume items for a few of their skills. Stacking 4 increases the Megalixir and High-Potion caps to 6 and 20.
-Merchants when they use a healing item have a chance to only partially consume it and leave behind a lower tier of the item. so using a High-Potion can get you a Mid-Potion instead of being fully consumed
-Harlequins whenever they use a thrown attack item have a chance to add it to the enemy's drop pool to reclaim them when the fight ends

My approach is like what
@LordOfPotatos
said - the limits are tied to the individual items themselves. (ex. 13x of the weakest potion, 7x of the mid level, etc.)
Weight management sucks even in the best of times, so an RPG Maker game that has it would just make the experience a slog because you're being forced to move slowly because you can't hoard things in the genre where hoarding things is typically a dopamine boost.
This already does enough to make the player scramble to use their items properly since they can't infinitely hold them.
My philosophy is to have low limits per item but a wide variety of items to choose from, since my gameplay loop is closer to Resident Evil (eg. needing to survive in dangerous gauntlets) than a typical Final Fantasy.
--
Beyond just item limits, I have other plans like:
- Poison preventing you from using Food items (since the implication is you're sick). Gotta use Medicine then. Also, non-human characters like robots can't eat food.
- Embargo status that prevents you from using items in general. Level 1 version only prevents that one character from doing so, but Level 2 prevents the entire party from accessing their inventory even from the menu.
- Items are treated as skills due to how I have my UI set up, so they're victim to Yanfly's Cooldowns and Limit uses.
This is more for equipment than your usable items, but I liked how FF4 had an entire dungeon where you had to wear non-metallic equipment because you'd get paralyzed otherwise.

It's a very good standard, and a lot of games would be improved if you did this, but I think we can still do better.
I would still like to see games with temporary item mechanics, example:
When you learn a poison skill, it also comes with a passive that generates 2 antidotes that can only be used in battle. Because someone who uses poison most likely has a means to cure it.
When you learn a poison resistance passive, it also generates 5 antidotes. Because even if YOU can ignore the poison, it's handy for helping out your allies and makes it so that not everyone in the party needs to take the same passive.
You can't buy antidotes. Specialty items just aren't available, or the components expire too quickly to carry around like a standard potion or bandage. This makes the rare Remedy or Panacea even more valuable, since anyone can use them regardless of equipped skills and it covers most/all status ailments.

Ooh. That's an interesting line of thinking. I think to really push the dungeon crawl I'd expand the "x per battle" uses to "x per long rest." But, if I wanted to stick with the more high fantasy action orientation of Chained Echoes, I'd do the per battle for sure.
Your point on item scarcity is important too, especially if you want to consider world building. There are really a lot of levers to pull to make a game more interesting, and it's a shame we so often go with "ultimate bag of holding."
Man, everyone's made some really good points. I'm glad I asked this question.

posts.author: Maliki79
posts.body:
I like
@LordOfPotatos
approach.
My only issue is communicating the various items maxes to the player.
So I do something similar in that I split items into broad categories: Battle items, equips and "other" items.
Equips you can only have one stack of, but you can carry I think 300 total.
So you can have 20 Iron Swords, but they each take up their own inventory slot. (Independent Items)
Battle items have their own category in my item menu and the player can only carry a max of 20 of each.
"Other" items have a cap of 9999 since most of those are used for crafting, trading or alternative currency.

Equip caps shouldn't be relevant aside from hardware/software limitations. You shouldn't actually be designing your game around needing to discard equipment when you get too many.
max 20 for consumables is a lot. Way more than a single boss battle, and it's not quite common to design attrition dungeons long enough to use up a full 20 of various items.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
NamEtag said:
Equip caps shouldn't be relevant aside from hardware/software limitations. You shouldn't actually be designing your game around needing to discard equipment when you get too many.
Click to expand...
I don't think that's a valid opinion to voice in that language - there's no justification for saying one "shouldn't" do it, as an objectively wrong thing.
There's absolutely nothing wrong with wanting to make your carrying capacity another form of resource management for how far you can get into a dungeon before having to retreat to town, just like your HP/MP/healing items typically are.
Also nothing wrong with wanting to have some aspect of realism, if you want to have weight/encumbrance playing a part in your game.
Further nothing wrong if you want the decision of which items to carry/bring/keep to be one of the strategic choices in your game.
It can be an aspect of games that you personally don't like - I don't like the way carrying capacity was implemented in, say, Skyrim - but if you're going to be a decent developer you should be able to understand the reasoning and value in design systems whether you would choose to implement them or not.
NamEtag said:
max 20 for consumables is a lot. Way more than a single boss battle, and it's not quite common to design attrition dungeons long enough to use up a full 20 of various items.
Click to expand...
That's a pretty random and arbitrary thing to claim. How can you say that knowing zero things about what the items do, how much they heal, how battles or boss battles work, etc.?
I'm replaying Final Fantasy Dimensions, and in the last dungeon - between potions, status curatives, and a few tents - I absolutely spent more than 20 items.

posts.author: mauvebutterfly
posts.body:
My game is a puzzle game that is about resource management. Each time your character goes on a mission they bring their standard loadout of consumable items with them, and the player needs to decide how best to use the resources to navigate the environment and achieve their objective.
The most obvious item limit is only having 6 arrows. The main character is an archer, so planning how best to use your limited ammunition is important. Arrows can be fired on the main map outside of combat, but in combat they are your most effective attack. In combat, a combat event checks for arrows at the start of each turn and will enable or disable the archery skill as appropriate.
Other items are gathered on-site, so killing an animal will give you meat, which you can then use to try to lure animals around to get past them without fighting. Alternatively, eating the meat restores health. Getting to a campsite lets you cook the meat increasing its healing value.
I think this approach only really works since I'm doing a puzzle game. There are some limited powerups and stat increases, but your inventory is reset for each mission, so it isn't possible to hoard a lot of items.

Sure, consider it a blanket arbitrary statement that has exceptions. If you know enough about the exception to outline why you wouldn't follow what I said, you probably know enough to do so.
As for max. 20: Using 50 potions and 25 antidotes is possible, but I'd say that's far from ideal for a system that's trying to enforce item caps. The whole point is to limit you, and 20 is a lot for most items. Using 10 ethers is already quite luxurious. Yes, it is a blanket generalization and surely has exceptions. But I find an answer like this is more useful than "it depends".

posts.author: Maliki79
posts.body:
@NamEtag
Fair enough points.
I use YFs item core to grant independent items for weapons and armors, so there is technically a software limitation imposed on me.
That said, there's a grand total of 90 weapons and 60 armors in my game with the vast majority of them being special one-time drops or finds.  That inventory cap is there to encourage players to utilize my equipment building system while still giving room to purchase a few copies of purchasable equipment, which is probably only going to have relevance in the early game. (The found gear and equips you power up will far surpass most purchasable items mid-game.)
As for the battle items, it is a simple case of resource management.  Spamming regular attacks will not end battles quickly in my game.
Skills which cost MP usually are required for effectively finishing battles.  (And all enemies drop different items based on kills vs a specific element, so using spells is almost a given.) So while my early dungeons don't tax your resources too much, later dungeons will push the player to figure out strategies to complete dungeons while maintaining items.
I do have an item crafting system that can make more items in dungeons.  However, the items to make advanced healing items are the basic ones, so the players will only be able to take that but so far. Think 5 potions to make 1 hi-potion.  5-hi-potions to make 1 max-potion. And this goes for the MP restoration potions as well.
I hope I explained that well enough.
Open to continue the discussion as it might help with me tweaking things.
(And you can always opt to try my game too and critique it directly. )

posts.author: SundialShark
posts.body:
Like the others have already stated, I go for the "Limit Only Certain Stacks" approach, except I make it clear that town building materials can go up to 999, and other items like consumables and cooking materials have a much lower count by changing the number from a solid white to gold to tell the player they can't collect anymore of that thing (this shot's a bad example of that, but most items don't go past 99 let alone maybe 50 or 30 unless they're a building material, even less if its a food item that is ready to eat). Then I add a sorting system to make it even clearer. My equipments (also independent items) don't stack either as I try to encourage players to level up their weapons and increase their Style Level, an overall gear level metric, since they cannot naturally level up characters traditionally through EXP. It all gets soaked into the weapon.
I try to think about the relationship between items and the purpose of the tension of having limited resources that you want to begin with.

I'm making a narrative game with a just a few mechanics, and the few items you get are easily remembered. Options and saving the game can be accessed at certain points. (Think save crystals.)

posts.author: freakytapir
posts.body:
I'll be honest. An inventory is a means to an end in my view. As someone who has spent last week playing inventory tetris among 6 different characters in Baldur's gate 2 (yes, Two, not Three), what I want is for the inventory sytem to be efficient and effective.
Now, Final Fantay 16 had a lot wrong with it in some areas but I did like the very limited amount of consumables you could carry. You pick up a potion while already having four in your inentory? the one picked up gets used instantaneously.
Kind of also reminds me of Kingdom hearts where you have to equip items from an out of combat inventory to use in battle, restocking between battles from the main one.
